A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Rubric Reward Model study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including material moved between the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original model-training experiments, mathematical benchmark evaluations, direct-answer probes, and human assessments of reasoning errors and automated judging.

after.justification: V3 retains these original empirical results and adds answer-candidate examples and an analysis relating response length to verified correctness.

M1.justification: The three-phase pipeline remains unchanged: Gemini-generated rubrics, scored-response synthesis, and SFT followed by PPO for the RRM. The scoring objective and downstream rubric-reward training are retained. V3 summarizes the method and moves its detailed description to Appendix D.3.

E1.justification: Both versions use the Polaris training subset and evaluate AIME2024, MATH500, AMC2023, and OlympiadBench, including the existing challenge set and full-dataset evaluations. V3's answer-space examples describe retained benchmarks; coding and scientific reasoning are discussed only as possible extensions.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparators remain the outcome-reward baseline, ReasonFlux-PRM-7B, the Qwen3-4B false-positive verifier, and the same four leading models. The proposed comparison against Gemini scoring without rubrics is explicitly unperformed.

E3.justification: The training budgets, decoding settings, detection thresholds, Standard and Verified Pass@N metrics, subset/full-dataset design, and challenge-set evaluation protocol are retained. The added descriptive analyses do not document revised settings or additional experimental controls.

E4.justification: V3 adds answer-space and beam-candidate examinations in Tables 2–3 and a response-length versus verified-correctness analysis in Section 5.3. Existing error distributions, SFT-versus-PPO analyses, judge validation, and case studies remain. These are limited supplementary additions, without a controlled teacher-model ablation.

E5.justification: Both versions retain five-run scoring-stability checks, the full-dataset 32-run statement, and Pearson correlation reporting for rubric reward versus false-positive rate (v1 Figure 3b; v3 Figure 4b). The added length correlation extends an existing statistical reporting practice; no new uncertainty estimates, significance tests, or seed information appear.

E6.justification: V3 newly reports a length–verified-correctness correlation of -0.24 and the answer/candidate entries in Tables 2–3. Existing benchmark curves, comparator scores, error counts, and human-validation results remain unchanged, including the reported AIME2024 Verified Pass@1024 comparison of 26.7% versus 62.6%.

T1.justification: The normalized absolute-score-error reward and dataset constructions retain the same mathematical meaning. V3 changes notation and placement but adds no substantive definitions, assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion reframe Miracle Steps around answer-recall shortcuts, with memorization among several possible contributors, instead of emphasizing memorization primarily. The taxonomy, RRM contribution, and headline effectiveness claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 3.2 substantially expands the mechanism discussion to consider simplicity, guessability, approximation heuristics, and memorization. Section 4.1 and Limitations newly acknowledge the teacher-model confound and explain possible advantages of explicit rubrics. Section 5.3 also adds an argument against verbosity-based reward hacking. These materially broaden interpretation and limitations beyond v1's existing causality caveat.

D1.justification: Appendix D.1 newly identifies the annotators as recruited PhD students paid $27.5 per hour, and Section 4.1 adds estimated teacher-call costs. Prompts, hyperparameters, hardware details, and the code/data availability statement are retained despite removal of the standalone reproducibility summary.

R1.justification: V3 adds Dineen et al.'s QA-lign and Guo et al.'s Mathematical Proof as a Litmus Test. It explicitly positions its broader mathematical problems and answer spaces against the latter's proof-failure analysis. The main related-work framework otherwise remains intact.

P1.justification: V3 rewrites the mechanism discussion, condenses the main method description, and relocates the taxonomy-analysis pipeline and detailed RRM construction to appendices. It also restructures the appendices and rewrites the conclusion and limitations. This is substantial narrative reorganization beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: V3 adopts a two-column layout, adds Tables 2–3, captions the existing motivating example as Figure 2, and redraws several diagnostic plots. It transposes the leading-model table, moves the overall confusion matrix to the appendix, and combines v1 Figures 9–11 into Figure 10a–c.

improvement.justification: V3 modestly improves transparency through competing explanations, concrete probing examples, and explicit acknowledgment of the teacher-model confound. These help readers interpret the retained results without resolving the central causal questions. The gain is limited by an overstatement: the new negative length–correctness correlation does not by itself rule out verbosity-based reward hacking.
